DC vs 1-phase AC vs 3-phase AC — every formula side by side

The same three questions are asked in every circuit sum: how much current, how much power, how much loss/drop. DC answers them with R alone. 1-phase AC adds the reactance X, so the angle φ (power factor) enters. 3-phase AC is just three 1-phase circuits — solve ONE phase, then multiply by 3 (or use √3 with line values). Picture: DC = water pushed steadily by a pump; 1-phase AC = water sloshing back and forth; 3-phase = three pumps taking turns 120° apart, so the total push never drops.

3. How to solve a sum — step by step

DC sum

1. Draw the circuit; L = short, C = open (steady state).

2. Series/parallel, KCL/KVL, Thevenin as needed.

3. I = V/R.

4. P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

5. Loss/drop: count go AND return conductor (2R).

1-phase AC sum

1. Find XL = 2πfL, XC = 1/(2πfC).

2. Z = R + j(XL − XC), |Z|, φ = tan⁻¹(X/R).

3. I = V/|Z| (use rms V).

4. pf = cos φ = R/|Z| (lag if XL > XC).

5. P = I²R, Q = I²X, S = VI; check S² = P² + Q².

3-phase AC sum

1. Note star or delta; get Vph (star: VL/√3).

2. Delta load? Convert to star (Z/3) OR solve the delta phase directly.

3. Solve ONE phase like a 1-phase sum: Iph = Vph/|Zph|.

4. Line current: star = Iph, delta = √3 Iph.

5. Total = 3 × per-phase power (or √3 VLIL cos φ).

6b. Supply systems compared — how much conductor material?

Same power P, same line loss, same length and the same maximum voltage to earth Vm (the insulation limit). Copper (or aluminium) volume is counted relative to the 2-wire DC system with one conductor earthed. AC values are for unity pf — divide by cos²φ for any other pf.

Read it like this: DC 2-wire mid-point earthed needs only ¼ of the base copper (the wire-to-wire voltage doubles, so the current halves and the loss falls to ¼). 3-φ 3-wire needs 0.5/cos²φ — four times less than 1-φ 2-wire (2/cos²φ) on this basis. On the other common basis (same voltage between conductors), 1-φ 2-wire = 1/cos²φ and 3-φ 3-wire = 0.75/cos²φ (table 1, last row). Copper loss of a DC 2-wire mid-point earthed line (R per wire, V to earth): I = P/2V, loss = 2I²R = P²R/(2V²).

PART B — Transformer, DC, synchronous and induction machines side by side

Every rotating machine is ONE idea used two ways: a generator turns motion into EMF (E is bigger than V, current flows OUT), a motor turns EMF-against-supply into motion (V is bigger than E, current flows IN). Change the sign of the internal drop and you switch between generator and motor. The transformer is the same EMF law with nothing rotating.

11. How to solve each machine sum

DC machine

1. Generator: E = V + IaRa; motor: Eb = V − IaRa (Ia = IL ± Ish).

2. Two conditions → E ∝ ΦN.

3. Torque ∝ ΦIa; power E Ia = Tω.

4. Series motor: Φ ∝ Ia.

Transformer

1. Ratio a = N1/N2; refer Z by a².

2. OC → core loss; SC → Cu loss & Zeq.

3. Cu loss at load x: x²Pcu,FL.

4. η = out/(out + Pi + x²Pcu); reg = εr cos φ ± εx sin φ.

Synchronous / induction

1. Work per PHASE (Vph = VL/√3 for star).

2. Sync: phasor E = V ± jXsI (lag/lead angle of I matters) → δ → P = EV sin δ/Xs × 3.

3. Induction: Ns → s → Pag split 1 : s : (1 − s) → T = Pag/ωs.
